instr: Use the ∫ template on the calculator screen, or ∫f(x)dx on the graph.

You have two tries; then we show the answer.

steps.worked:
\(\displaystyle\int_0^3 x^{2}e^{-x}\,dx=1.15\)   (\(1.1536\))
the shaded area under the curve from \(0\) to \(3\)
steps.ok: ✓ \(1.15\) is right. The lesson covers where the tool lives, what the number means, and when area is not the same as the integral.

steps.title: The definite integral is a number the GDC gives you
steps.body:
Three facts to hold:
•  \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) is the signed area between the curve and the \(x\)-axis from \(a\) to \(b\)
•  the GDC gives it directly: the ∫ template on the calculator screen, or ∫f(x)dx on the graph
•  above the axis counts positive, below counts negative

The shaded region here is \(\int_0^3 x^{2}e^{-x}\,dx=1.15\): entirely above the axis, so the integral and the area agree.

steps.title: The GDC says \(\int_{-1}^{2}(x^{3}-x)\,dx=2.25\). Is \(2.25\) the area between the curve and the \(x\)-axis?
opts: No: between \(0\) and \(1\) the curve is below the axis, so that piece was subtracted. The area is larger than \(2.25\).
Yes: the integral is always the area.
No: the area is smaller, because part of the curve is below the axis.
steps.ok: ✓ Right. The piece below the axis counted negative in the integral; for the area it must count positive. Area \(=2.75\).
bads: ✗ The integral is the signed area: below the axis counts negative. Here the piece from \(0\) to \(1\) was subtracted, so the area is more than \(2.25\).
✗ The area counts every piece as positive, so it is bigger than the integral, not smaller: \(2.75\).

steps.title: Area: make every piece positive
steps.body:
When the question says area (or the curve dips below the axis):
•  find the zeros between the limits: here \(x=0\) and \(x=1\)
•  integrate \(|f(x)|\) on the GDC, or integrate each piece and add the sizes

\(\int_{-1}^{2}|x^{3}-x|\,dx=0.25+0.25+2.25=2.75\), while \(\int_{-1}^{2}(x^{3}-x)\,dx=0.25-0.25+2.25=2.25\).

A sketch with the region shaded earns the method mark even if the value slips. The integral statement must have limits and \(dx\); “area = 2.75” alone is an answer without method.

steps.title: Area between two curves: top minus bottom
steps.body:
For the region between \(y=2x+3\) and \(y=x^{2}\):
•  intersection tool first: \(x=-1\) and \(x=3\); these are the limits
•  integrate (top curve) − (bottom curve) between them: \(\int_{-1}^{3}\big((2x+3)-x^{2}\big)\,dx\)
•  the GDC gives \(10.7\) (\(=\tfrac{32}{3}\))

If the curves cross again inside the region, the “top” swaps: use \(|\text{top}-\text{bottom}|\) to be safe.

parts: The limits of the integral are
✗ The region runs from one crossing to the other along the \(x\)-axis: limits \(-1\) and \(3\).
Which is on top between the crossings?
✗ At \(x=0\) the line gives \(3\) and the parabola \(0\): the line is on top throughout.

\(20\) is \(\int_{-1}^{3}(2x+3)\,dx\): the parabola was not subtracted.

steps.title: Models: the integral of a rate is a total
steps.body:
Water flows into a tank at \(r(t)=20e^{-0.1t}\) litres per minute.
•  “how much water in the first \(10\) minutes?” means \(\int_0^{10}r(t)\,dt\)
•  rate × time = amount; the integral adds up rate × tiny time over the interval
•  the answer has the units of the amount (litres), not the rate

\(\int_0^{10}20e^{-0.1t}\,dt=126\) litres.

parts: ✓ The integral of the rate over the time.
✗ Total amount \(=\int\) rate \(dt\) over the interval: \(\int_0^{10}20e^{-0.1t}\,dt\).
steps.givenNote: rate of flow in litres per minute, \(t\) minutes after the tap is opened
steps.title: Find the amount of water that flows into the tank in the first \(10\) minutes.
instr: Type the amount in litres to 3 significant figures.
steps.label: litres \(=\)
wrongs: \(7.36\) is the rate at \(t=10\), not the total.
\(200\) is the total if the tap ran for ever (\(\int_0^{\infty}\)); stop at \(10\).
That is the total divided by \(10\): the integral already is the total.

parts: The curves cross inside the interval at
\(x=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\): cos is on top before it, sin after
✓ So top minus bottom swaps at \(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\).
✗ \(\sin x=\cos x\) at \(x=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\) (\(0.785\)); after that sine is on top.
✗ Without the absolute value the two pieces partly cancel. Use \(|\sin x-\cos x|\), or split at \(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the zeros of \(f\). Enter the two non-zero ones, smaller first.
parts.figCap: Zero tool at each crossing (or factorise: x(x − 1)(x − 3)).
wrongs: \(0\) is a zero, but the boxes ask for the other two: \(1\) and \(3\).
\(f(2)=-2\), not a zero.

parts.label: (b)
parts.figCap: The integral counts the region below the axis as negative: 0.417 − 2.667 = −2.25.
wrongs: Sign: more of the region is below the axis than above, so the integral is negative.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the total area of the regions enclosed by the curve and the \(x\)-axis.
parts.figCap: Two regions between the zeros: 0.417 above the axis, 2.667 below. Area = 3.08.
wrongs: That is the integral; for the area every piece counts positive.
The integral’s size is not the area: \(0.417+2.667=3.08\).

The integral tool on the GDC is only approximate
The area should be the integral squared
parts.bad: The integral is a signed area: the region below the axis (from \(1\) to \(3\)) is subtracted in (b) but added in (c).

questions.stem: The region \(R\) is enclosed by the curve \(y=4-x^{2}\) and the line \(y=x+2\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the \(x\)-coordinates of the points where the curve and the line meet.
wrongs: \(2\) is a zero of the curve, not a crossing with the line.
\(3\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of the second crossing.

parts.label: (b)

ft.$fn: function (a, b) { var g = function (x) { return 4 - x * x - x - 2; }; var n = 60, h = (b - a) / n, s = 0; for (var i = 0; i <= n; i++) s += (i === 0 || i === n ? 1 : (i % 2 ? 4 : 2)) * g(a + i * h); return Math.abs(s * h / 3); }

parts.figCap: Curve on top between the crossings: ∫ (curve − line) from −2 to 1.
ms: correct integrand and limits (curve on top: at \(x=0\), \(4>2\))
wrongs: Sign: line minus curve. The curve is on top between the crossings.
\(9\) is \(\int_{-2}^{1}(4-x^{2})\,dx\): the line was not subtracted.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the area of the region between the curve \(y=4-x^{2}\) and the \(x\)-axis for \(1\le x\le3\).
parts.figCap: The curve crosses the axis at x = 2 inside the interval: 1.667 above, 2.333 below. Area = 4.
parts.note: The region in (c) changes side at \(x=2\); the plain integral \(\int_1^3(4-x^{2})\,dx=-0.667\) is not the area.
wrongs: \(-0.667\) is \(\int_1^3(4-x^{2})\,dx\): the pieces partly cancelled.
The size of the integral is not the area: \(1.67+2.33=4\).
\(1.67\) is the piece from \(1\) to \(2\) only.

questions.stem: Water flows into a tank at a rate of \(r(t)=10e^{-0.15t}+1\) litres per minute, where \(t\) is the time in minutes after the tap is opened, for \(0\le t\le20\). The tank is empty at \(t=0\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write down the rate of flow when the tap is opened.
wrongs: \(1\) is the long-run rate, as \(t\to\infty\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the volume of water in the tank after \(20\) minutes.
parts.figCap: Volume = ∫ rate dt: the shaded area under r(t) from 0 to 20.
wrongs: \(1.50\) is the rate at \(t=20\), not the volume.
\(30\) is \(r(20)\times20\): the rate is not constant; integrate.
\(63.3\) is \(\int_0^{20}10e^{-0.15t}\,dt\): the \(+1\) contributes \(20\) more litres.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the time at which the tank contains \(50\) litres of water.
parts.figCap: Graph V(t) = ∫₀ᵗ r(u) du with y = 50; intersection at t = 6.93.
ms: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{T}r(t)\,dt=50\): graph the integral with \(T\) as the upper limit (or use the solver)
parts.note: The unknown is the upper limit. Graph \(y=\int_0^{x}r(t)\,dt\) and \(y=50\), or solve the equation with the solver.
wrongs: \(4.55\) is \(50\div11\): the rate is not constant.
\(50\) is the volume, not the time.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The rate of flow decreases throughout. State, with a reason, whether the volume of water in the tank is increasing or decreasing.
opts: Increasing: the rate is always positive, so water keeps entering even though it enters more slowly
Constant: the rate levels off at 1
parts.bad: The volume is the integral of the rate. A positive rate means the volume keeps increasing; a decreasing rate only means it increases more slowly.
ms: increasing, since \(r(t)>0\) for all \(t\) (the rate is positive even though it is decreasing)

apply.lostMarksHint: most lost marks here are giving the integral when the area was asked (or the reverse), not splitting at a zero inside the interval, and reporting a rate instead of a total.
